The Department of Justice and federal courts have interpreted injury not to require any physical act or harm. You can be injured by being defrauded or tricked or by having your right taken from you without any violence at all. Prosecutions for ballot box stuffing, for example, have survived motions to dismiss. In US v. Sailor, 322 US 385, 1944, the trial court threw out the indictments of elected officials charged with stuffing the ballot box, and the Supreme Court reversed, holding that ballot stuffing injures the constitutional right to have your vote honestly counted. So, the question is this, can you injure someone in their constitutional right to vote by deceiving them about which candidate they are actually voting for? That is, by tricking them into voting for the wrong candidate when they intend to vote for someone else. The statute and the law case and the and the case law say yes. Mackie is the closest modern analog, and like the operatives here, Douglas Mackie was a private actor, not an election official. In Stone, county election supervisors in Maryland were alleged to have printed and folded the official ballots in such a form that any voter could easily vote for the Democratic candidate, while making it difficult for any of the illiterate Negro voters to vote for the Republican candidate. And that's a quote, by the way, from the actual Supreme Court. ID at 83 at 838. The court held that this was sufficient to allege any injury under the predecessor statute of code 241. It said, quote, "Unlawfully to deprive a citizen of the United of the United States of his right to vote at a congressional election is to injure him in any ordinary use of the word." Mackie's conviction, of course, was reversed by the second circuit, but on the grounds that there was no evidence he entered into any kind of conspiracy or agreement, not that there wasn't a cognizable injury. The right at issue is best understood as the constitutional right to vote for the candidate of your choice. Trickery, deception, and fraud carried out through the mechanics of voting, including how the ballot itself appears or is printed, are sufficient to allege an injury to that right.
